nodes.label: Micro-benchmarking with BenchmarkDotNet
nodes.rationale: It handles JIT warmup, tiered compilation, outlier detection, statistical significance, allocation tracking and dead-code elimination — all of which hand-rolled Stopwatch code gets wrong below about a millisecond. Never point it at an HTTP endpoint: no concurrency, no pooling, no realistic contention, and it measures a network hop as if it were code. That is a category error worth being able to name.

nodes.label: Load testing the whole system
nodes.rationale: Benchmarking finds slow code; load testing finds slow systems. A method benchmarking at 50 ns can still produce an endpoint that collapses at 100 concurrent users, because the bottleneck was the connection pool, a lock, or thread-pool starvation — none of which exist in a single-threaded benchmark. Its cost is an environment resembling production; load testing an empty database tells you almost nothing.

nodes.label: A benchmark whose conditions you cannot state is a number, not evidence
nodes.rationale: The committed reports came from a 4-core shared cloud VM under a ShortRun job, so some Error values are the same order as the Mean. Fine for order-of-magnitude claims (11x, 1,857x), not for anything subtler — two results within 2x on this hardware are 'about the same'. Saying that is worth more in an interview than a table of impressive figures.

nodes.label: Dependency licence screening
nodes.rationale: BenchmarkDotNet is MIT and free commercially; NBomber moved to a paid commercial subscription (licence v3.0, September 2025) so the planned dependency was replaced with a small purpose-built harness in tests/Bank.LoadTests; k6 is AGPL-3.0 and its scripts are committed. Same reasoning that removed MediatR and FluentAssertions — a public teaching repo should not carry dependencies a reader cannot use at work.

nodes.label: Profile, benchmark, load test, measure in production
nodes.rationale: Do not benchmark what you have not proven is hot. Profile first (dotnet-trace, dotnet-counters), benchmark the hot method once identified, load test the system because the bottleneck usually is not the method, then measure in production. Most real problems are found at the last two steps; the satisfying numbers are at step 2, which is exactly why people over-invest there.
